passage:
School counsellor's note, Monday.

This morning, from the staff room window, I saw Jasleen from class ten crossing the school lane while typing on her phone. She was looking at the road now and then, but her thumbs never stopped. A cyclist rang his bell twice and swerved; she didn't react until he was almost past. Then she nearly stepped into the open drain by the gate. Her friend Alka pulled her back by the bag strap.

I called both girls in at lunch. Jasleen said, "But I was looking!" I explained that eyes can point at the road while the mind is inside the phone. We agreed on a simple habit: stop at the gate, finish the message, then walk. I have also asked the office to get the drain covered this week.

qa.q: What did Jasleen nearly step into?
qa.a: She nearly stepped into the open drain by the gate.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen insist "But I was looking!"?
qa.a: She felt genuinely surprised and a bit defensive, because her eyes were on the road now and then, so she believed she had seen everything.

qa.q: What habit did the counsellor and the girls agree on, and why might it work?
qa.a: Stop at the gate, finish the message, then walk, so her attention is fully on the road while crossing.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt when she pulled Jasleen back?
qa.a: Alka was probably frightened for her friend and relieved she grabbed the bag strap in time.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teenager texting while walking who misses a cyclist and a drain, because looking isn't seeing when attention is elsewhere.

passage:
Thursday night

Almost walked into Raghav bhaiya's scooter today. I was texting Mira about the maths test on the way back from tuition. I KNOW I looked up at the corner. I saw the road. Then suddenly a horn and bhaiya shouting "Uma!" and his brakes squealing right next to me.

He wasn't even angry after, just pale. He said, "You looked straight at me." I don't remember seeing him at all. How is that possible??

My heart was banging all the way home. I think my eyes were on the road but my head was in the chat.

New rule for me: phone in bag when I'm walking. If a message can't wait two minutes, I stop on the footpath first. Told Mummy about it at dinner and she's going to remind me.

qa.q: Whose scooter did Uma almost walk into?
qa.a: Raghav bhaiya's scooter.

qa.q: How did Uma feel after the near miss, and what shows it?
qa.a: Uma was frightened and shaken, with a heart banging all the way home, and confused about not seeing the scooter.

qa.q: Is Uma's new rule a good one? Why?
qa.a: Yes, keeping the phone in the bag and stopping on the footpath means attention stays on the road while walking.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when Uma looked straight at him but still stepped out?
qa.a: Raghav was probably scared and shocked, which is why he was pale rather than angry.

grounding: A teenager walking while texting misses a scooter in plain view, as looking isn't seeing when attention is elsewhere.

Aditi had passed her driving test a month ago. That evening she was driving her aunt Noor's car to the pharmacy in heavy rain, wipers thumping, and her phone buzzed with a call from her project group.

She answered on speaker. "Yes, I'll send the slides tonight..."

At the zebra crossing, a man with a black umbrella was already halfway across. She saw the lights. She saw the road. She didn't see him until Noor shouted, "Stop!"

Aditi slammed the brakes. The man jumped back, shaken, and waved his umbrella at her.

Her hands were trembling on the wheel. She ended the call, pulled over by the pharmacy, and put her phone in the glove box. "I was looking straight ahead," she whispered.

qa.q: Who was crossing at the zebra crossing?
qa.a: A man with a black umbrella was already halfway across.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she whispered "I was looking straight ahead"?
qa.a: She felt frightened and shaken, and confused that she missed him while her eyes were on the road.

qa.q: What did Aditi do right after the near miss, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She ended the call, pulled over and put her phone in the glove box, so calls can't pull her attention while driving.

qa.q: How might the man with the umbrella have felt?
qa.a: He was probably scared and angry, having nearly been hit while crossing properly.

grounding: A young driver on a call misses a pedestrian in plain view, a limit of attention that habits must guard against.

passage:
Anand had driven the same road in Bengaluru every day for a year, to his job at the bakery supply store. He knew every pothole.

That Tuesday he was checking a delivery route on the map app while waiting at the signal. When it turned green, he glanced up, pressed the accelerator, and looked down again.

A small boy crossing with his father stepped off the kerb. Anand's colleague Asif, in the passenger seat, yelled. Anand braked hard, missing the boy by an arm's length.

The father held the boy tight and stared at him. Anand felt his face burn.

"I'm not a careless person," he told Asif later, still shaking. "I just thought I could look quickly."

That evening he set the route before starting and mounted the phone out of reach.

qa.q: How far was the boy from the car when Anand braked?
qa.a: He missed the boy by an arm's length.

qa.q: Why did Anand tell Asif "I'm not a careless person"?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and shaken, and wanted to explain that he thought a quick look was harmless, not that he didn't care.

qa.q: What changes did Anand make, and why do they help?
qa.a: He set the route before starting and put the phone out of reach, so habit protects his attention instead of willpower.

qa.q: What might the father have felt holding the boy tight?
qa.a: The father was probably terrified and angry, relieved his son was safe.

grounding: A young driver checking an app misses a pedestrian in plain view, a limit of attention that needs habits to guard against.

Sumit ran the small electrical workshop in his town near Kolhapur. Every morning before the first job, he put his phone in a steel box by the door.

"You'll miss orders," his cousin Seema said, visiting one day.

"Orders can wait twenty minutes. Wiring can't."

That afternoon, Sumit was fixing the panel at the village school. He didn't look at his phone once. Before switching the power back on, he called his helper over. "Check my connections."

The helper found one loose wire. Sumit tightened it and nodded.

On the drive home, the phone stayed in the glove box. Seema watched him, arms folded, then smiled. "Your hands are steady because your head isn't elsewhere, isn't it?"

qa.q: Where does Sumit put his phone every morning?
qa.a: In a steel box by the door.

qa.q: Why does Sumit feel calm ignoring his phone while working?
qa.a: He feels sure that orders can wait but wiring can't, so he's comfortable giving the job his full attention.

qa.q: What did Sumit do before switching the power back on, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He asked his helper to check his connections, and a second pair of eyes caught a loose wire.

qa.q: How does Seema's view change during the day?
qa.a: Seema is doubtful at first but later seems impressed, seeing how his focus keeps his work steady.

grounding: A wise worker keeps the phone away during driving and critical work, and has a second person double-check.

In Oslo, Bilal worked as a junior pharmacist. His colleague Astrid noticed that before every prescription check, he turned his phone face down in a drawer.

"You're very strict about that," she said.

"When I'm reading doses, I want nothing else in my head."

Later that day, Bilal met a worried mother at the counter who wanted to talk about her son's medicine. He left the drawer shut and listened to her, not glancing away once.

At the end of the shift, he handed Astrid a tricky order. "Can you check this with me?"

She found nothing wrong. "You didn't need me."

"This time," Bilal said. "The day I think I don't need a second check is the day I miss something."

qa.q: Where did Bilal put his phone before prescription checks?
qa.a: He turned it face down in a drawer.

qa.q: Why does Bilal still ask Astrid to check even when she finds nothing wrong?
qa.a: He feels humble and cautious, knowing that feeling sure isn't the same as being right on important work.

qa.q: What made Bilal's conversation with the worried mother go well?
qa.a: He kept his phone away and listened without glancing away, giving her his full attention.

qa.q: How might the mother at the counter have felt?
qa.a: She probably felt heard and reassured by his full attention.

grounding: A wise worker keeps the phone away for critical checks and key conversations and double-checks with a colleague.

"I work better like this," he told his friend Jin, who had come over to study.

Jin did her list in silence. Twenty minutes later she closed her book. "Done. Test me?"

Yosef was on word six. Every time a robot exploded on screen, he stopped writing and laughed.

They tested each other. Jin got nineteen out of twenty. Yosef got eleven.

"The robots were loud," he muttered.

"You said you could do both," said Jin.

Yosef looked at the screen, then at his list. He turned the tablet over, and started again from word one.

"I'm being productive," he told his mother. "I'm replying and studying."

He read the first line of the paragraph on acids. Buzz. He answered Mohit. Back to acids. Where was he? He read the line again.

The next evening, he left the phone in the living room for forty minutes. Mohit's messages piled up. Amandeep got through five pages.

Last year in class nine, I thought I was a genius at multitasking. I'd have my history notes open, and every time my friend Rafiq messaged about football, I'd answer straight away. It felt great, like I was keeping up with everything.

Then one night I timed myself. Every reply took maybe thirty seconds. But getting back into the Mughal chapter took much longer. I'd reread the same paragraph, forget whose reign I was on, and scroll up again. In one hour, I'd done about fifteen minutes of real study.

Now I put the phone on the shelf for forty minutes and tell Rafiq I'll reply at the break. He sends a thumbs-up and waits.

I'm Tanvir. I'm not a genius at multitasking. Nobody is, I think.

qa.q: How much real study did Tanvir do in one hour?
qa.a: About fifteen minutes of real study.

qa.q: Why did answering Rafiq straight away feel good to Tanvir?
qa.a: It felt exciting and satisfying, like keeping up with everything, so Tanvir didn't notice the time lost getting back into the chapter.

qa.q: What does Tanvir do now, and why does it work?
qa.a: Tanvir puts the phone on the shelf for forty minutes and replies at the break, so there are fewer switches that break focus.

qa.q: How does Rafiq respond to Tanvir's new routine?
qa.a: Rafiq sends a thumbs-up and waits, so he seems fine with it and understanding.

grounding: A teenager who replied to messages while studying realises each switch cost focus and time to get back into the topic.

passage:
In a crowded seminar room in Mumbai, Sumit sat at the back with his laptop: slides in one window, a group chat in another, a video paused in a third. He felt sharp and busy.

The lecturer, Dr Madhuri, stopped mid-sentence. "Sumit, what did I just say about the second method?"

Sumit blinked. He had heard her voice the whole time. "The... second method is... better?"

A few people laughed. His ears burned.

After class, he checked his notes. There were bits of three lectures mixed up, and one line that said "ask about lunch."

The next week, he closed everything but the slides and a blank page. For the first time in weeks, he could explain the lecture to his roommate.

qa.q: What did Dr Madhuri ask Sumit about?

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when his ears burned?

qa.a: He closed everything but the slides and a blank page, so his attention stayed with the lecture.

Pradeep had a client report due by five, his daughter's school had called twice, and the office printer was broken. It was already noon.

His colleague Karthik watched him put his phone on silent, close his email, and set a timer for fifty minutes.

"What if your daughter's school calls again?"

At 4:15 he sent the report. Karthik, still halfway through his own, sighed. "How?"

"Fewer switches," Pradeep said. "That's all."

Every morning at nine, Kashish closed the door of her small room at the architecture firm in Pune. Notifications off, one drawing on the screen.

Her new colleague Alka found it odd. "Don't you check messages?"

"At eleven and at three," Kashish said. "All at once."

Alka tried to work like everyone else, with chat open and email pinging. By lunch she had started three drawings and finished none.

Kashish had finished the first floor plan and gone for a short walk.

"I used to work like you," Kashish told her. "I thought I was fast. I was just busy."

The next morning, Alka closed her chat for an hour. It felt strange at first. By eleven, she had a whole elevation done.

qa.q: At what times does Kashish check messages?
qa.a: At eleven and at three.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt by lunch with three drawings started and none finished?
qa.a: She probably felt frustrated and a bit discouraged, working hard but getting little done.

qa.q: Which of Kashish's habits made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Checking messages only at set times, because it cut the switching that kept breaking her focus.

qa.q: What would change for Alka if she kept working in focused blocks?
qa.a: She would likely finish more drawings in less time and feel less scattered.

grounding: A productive professional works in single-task blocks, silences notifications, batches messages and rests.

passage:
Tarun ran a team of six at a Delhi marketing agency. At every weekly meeting, the same thing happened: people nodded while typing, then asked questions he had just answered.

He noticed it most with Hafsa, his best designer. She was always half on her laptop, and afterwards she messaged him: "What was the deadline again?"

One Monday, Tarun felt tired of repeating himself, but more than that, he felt they were wasting everyone's time.

"From now on, meetings are fifteen minutes, laptops shut," he said. "Bring a notebook if you want."

For two weeks, people fidgeted. By the third, Hafsa stopped messaging him afterwards. "I actually remember things now," she told him, a little surprised.

qa.q: How many people were on Tarun's team?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel about the half-listening at meetings?
qa.a: He felt tired of repeating himself and frustrated that everyone's time was being wasted.

qa.q: What did Tarun change, and why did it help?
qa.a: He made meetings fifteen minutes with laptops shut, so people gave full attention and remembered what was said.

qa.q: How did Hafsa experience the change?
qa.a: Hafsa was surprised and pleased that she actually remembered things and no longer had to ask afterwards.

grounding: A team lead sees colleagues half-listening while typing and sets short meetings with full attention.

passage:
"Nandini, can I be honest about the Monday meeting?"

"Sure, Jasleen. You're the lead."

"You were typing the whole time."

"I was listening. I just had a client email."

"Did you catch that we moved the launch?"

Nandini paused. "We moved the launch?"

"That's what I mean. Half the team does it, so the meeting drags and I repeat everything. I'm not angry. I get why. Everyone's swamped."

"So what do you want?"

"From Thursday, twenty-minute meetings. Laptops shut. Then everyone goes back to email."

"Twenty minutes? We never finish in an hour."

"Because nobody's really there."

Nandini laughed a little. "Fair."

On Thursday, they finished in eighteen minutes.

qa.q: How long did Thursday's meeting take?
qa.a: They finished in eighteen minutes.

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel about the team typing in meetings?
qa.a: Jasleen feels frustrated at repeating everything, but not angry, and is understanding that everyone is swamped.

qa.q: What worked in the way Jasleen raised the problem?
qa.a: Jasleen gave a clear example, the moved launch, and a simple new norm, which made it easy for Nandini to agree.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt on realising the launch change was missed?
qa.a: Nandini probably felt embarrassed and a little defensive at first, then open to the new rule.

grounding: A team lead notices colleagues half-listening while typing and sets a norm of short, fully attentive meetings.

passage:
"Abbu! In the Eid market I saw a big lion!"

Salma looked up from the vermicelli. "A lion, Abhinav?"

"Yes! A lion. He was eating ice cream."

"I think it was a man in a lion mask at the balloon stall."

"No, a real lion. With a crown. Like in my book."

"Your book has a lion with a crown?"

"Yes, the king lion!"

Salma smiled. Yesterday he'd said it was a small lion. Today it had a crown and ice cream.

"And tomorrow, will it fly?" she teased.

Abhinav thought seriously. "Maybe."

qa.q: What did Salma think Abhinav had really seen?
qa.a: A man in a lion mask at the balloon stall.

qa.q: Why was Abhinav so sure the lion was real and had a crown?
qa.a: He felt excited and sure, because the lion in his book had mixed into his memory and felt true to him.

qa.q: How could Salma gently help Abhinav with his story?
qa.a: She could enjoy the story with him while quietly mentioning what they both saw, without calling him a liar.

qa.q: How does Salma feel about the growing lion story?
qa.a: Salma seems amused and fond, noticing how the lion changes each time he tells it.

grounding: A preschooler retells an event and adds details from a storybook, reshaping the memory each time.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Diwali week, by the class teacher.

On Monday Baljeet told us a rocket at his colony party went "very high." By Wednesday it "flew into the moon." Today it had "a man inside, like the astronaut in our library book."

Hansa said, "No man!" Baljeet looked upset. "It did! I saw!"

I don't think he is fibbing; book pictures seem to join the memory. I asked him to draw his rocket, and I'll tell his parents. 🚀

qa.q: What did Baljeet say was inside the rocket today?
qa.a: A man inside, like the astronaut in the library book.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet look upset when Hansa disagreed?
qa.a: He felt hurt and frustrated, because to him the new details now felt like a real memory.

qa.q: Was the teacher's response a good one? Why?
qa.a: Yes, asking him to draw the rocket respected his story without calling it a lie, and telling his parents helps them understand.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Baljeet insisted?
qa.a: Hansa may have felt confused or cross, because she was sure there was no man in the rocket.

grounding: A teacher notes a preschooler whose retelling of a festival event grows with details from books, reshaping the memory.

passage:
It was the week of the village temple fair, and the monsoon had just ended. Tushar, five, came home and told his grandfather Yogesh, "I saw an elephant!"

The next day, telling his cousins, it was "a big elephant with a gold hat."

By the third day, at the tea shop, Tushar said, "The elephant picked me up with his trunk. Like in Dada's story."

Yogesh smiled. He had told Tushar that story last month, about his own boyhood.

"Did the elephant really pick you up?" he asked gently.

Tushar nodded hard. "Yes! I remember!"

Yogesh didn't argue. He just said, "Tell me what the elephant smelled like," and listened.

qa.q: Who told Tushar a story about an elephant last month?
qa.a: Yogesh, his grandfather, told it.

qa.q: Why did Tushar nod hard and say "I remember!"?
qa.a: He felt certain and excited, because the story he'd heard had become part of his memory of the fair.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do well when Tushar's story grew?
qa.a: He didn't argue or call it a lie; he kept listening and asked about the elephant, which kept Tushar feeling safe to talk.

qa.q: How might the cousins see Tushar's growing story?
qa.a: The cousins might be impressed or doubtful, depending on whether they were at the fair too.

grounding: A preschooler's retelling of a fair visit grows with details from a story he heard, reshaping the memory.

passage:
Sunday. Vasudha told Nani about their trip to Ooty: the toy train, the rose garden, the cold.

Wednesday. At dinner, her brother Omkar told the story too, adding a monkey that stole his sandwich on the train. Vasudha laughed with everyone.

The next Sunday, telling her friend on the phone, Vasudha said, "And a monkey grabbed my brother's sandwich right out of his hand on the toy train!" She could almost see it.

Later, Mummy looked at the photos. "Omkar, wasn't the monkey at the lake? After the train?"

Omkar shrugged. Vasudha frowned. She was sure it had been the train. She'd seen it, hadn't she? Or had she just heard it so many times?

qa.q: What did Omkar add to the story at dinner?
qa.a: A monkey that stole his sandwich on the train.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when Mummy said the monkey was at the lake?
qa.a: She felt confused and unsure, because the train version felt so real to her.

qa.q: What could Vasudha's family do to check memories of the trip?
qa.a: They could look at the photos together and talk about who remembers what, without deciding anyone is lying.

qa.q: How might Omkar see the confusion?
qa.a: Omkar just shrugs, so he may not care much or may not be sure himself.

grounding: A child retells a family trip with bits copied from a sibling's version and believes them, as memory is rebuilt each time.

passage:
Pradeep, you think your memory is a camera? Let your Himani Nani tell you something. When I was ten, we went by bus to my uncle's village for a wedding. I remembered a river crossing, a broken wheel, and my sister crying.

Every Diwali, my brothers told the story too, and each time they added something: a snake on the road, a man selling sugarcane, our father pushing the bus. By the time I was twelve, I told it with the snake and the sugarcane, and I truly remembered them.

Years later, my mother laughed. "There was no snake. That was your brother's joke."

I felt so strange. I could see that snake clearly! That's when I learnt that memories are built fresh each time you tell them.

qa.q: What did Himani's brothers add to the story?
qa.a: A snake on the road, a man selling sugarcane and their father pushing the bus.

qa.q: How did young Himani feel when her mother said there was no snake?
qa.a: Young Himani felt strange and unsettled, because the snake was so clear in memory.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Himani thought about memory?
qa.a: Her mother's laugh about the snake being a joke made Himani realise that memories are rebuilt each time they're told.

qa.q: How might Himani's brothers have seen their added details?
qa.a: They may have thought of them as jokes or fun additions, not realising their sister would come to remember them as real.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a child, she absorbed siblings' added details into her memory of a family trip.

passage:
The school had given the class just ten minutes to write about their summer holidays, and Gurleen, eleven, was scribbling fast. Her pencil kept breaking.

She wrote about the trip to Amritsar with her family: the golden temple, the langar, and "the man with the parrot who told our fortune."

At home, her older sister Irawati read it. "The parrot man? That was when you were asleep in the car. I told you about him."

"No, I saw him!" Gurleen said. "He had a green parrot and a red cloth."

"That's what I told you."

Gurleen went quiet. She could see the parrot so clearly. But she couldn't remember walking to him, or what he said.

qa.q: What did Gurleen write about the man with the parrot?
qa.a: The man with the parrot who told their fortune.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen go quiet after Irawati spoke?
qa.a: She felt confused and unsettled, realising the vivid memory might have come from Irawati's story, not her own eyes.

qa.q: What would you advise Gurleen when a memory feels vivid but others remember it differently?
qa.a: Talk it through calmly, check photos if there are any, and accept that memory can mix in what we've heard.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel when Gurleen insists she saw the parrot?
qa.a: Irawati might feel amused or a little frustrated, since she knows Gurleen was asleep.

grounding: Under time pressure, a child writes about a trip including details copied from her sister's version and believes them.
